new_statements.quote: Les tons ne sont malheureusement jamais notés, bien que Mrg Adam ait eu pleinement conscience de leur rôle linguistique. J'ai donc porté toute mon attention sur cet aspect-là de l'enregistrement. [fn. 6:] L'accent aigu marque un ton haut, l'accent grave un ton bas. L'apostrophe représente un ton H avec faille tonale. [...] L'accent circonflexe (^) indique un ton descendant et l'inflexe un ton montant. Une voyelle finale transcrite sans ton n'est pas prononcée. Sur les tons du ndumu, voir Puech (1987) où il est procédé à une comparaison avec un parler teke. [1987b, p. 165:] En ndumu au contraire le ton H se reporte sur la voyelle radicale : sg. cl. 1 bàlàgà / bálàgà "c'est un mâle".
new_statements.translation: Unfortunately tones are never marked [in Mgr Adam's Ndumu publications], although Mgr Adam was fully aware of their linguistic role. I have therefore given all my attention to that aspect of the recording. [fn. 6:] The acute accent marks a high tone, the grave accent a low tone. The apostrophe represents a H tone with downstep. [...] The circumflex indicates a falling tone and the inverted circumflex a rising tone. A final vowel transcribed without tone is not pronounced. On the tones of Ndumu see Puech (1987), where a comparison with a Teke variety is made. [1987b, p. 165:] In Ndumu, by contrast, the H tone is shifted onto the radical vowel: sg. cl. 1 bàlàgà / bálàgà 'it is a male'.
new_statements.citation: Puech, Gilbert. 1987a. La longue marche des ndumu. Pholia 2: 139-161 (p. 143 and fn. 6); and Puech, Gilbert. 1987b. Tons structurels et tons intonationnels en teke. Pholia 2: 163-173 (p. 165). Lyon: CRLS-Université Lumière Lyon 2.
new_statements.locator: Puech 1987a p. 143 (main text + footnote 6); Puech 1987b p. 165 (ex. 12-14), p. 166
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndumu is described as a two-tone language (H vs. B/L structural tones, with downstep, contour tones from tone concatenation, and intonational tones); tone is lexical and grammatical on noun and verb stems (verb radicals fall into B and H tone classes; a floating H shifts rightward onto the radical vowel in Ndumu, unlike Teke). Neither Puech article mentions stress, accent-as-prominence, or a stressed syllable; 'accent' occurs only as the name of the diacritics. No word-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal detail: floating H shifts to the radical vowel in Ndumu (bàlàgà -> bálàgà, mù:tù -> mú:tù) whereas Teke keeps it on the prefix and produces a mid tone/downstep; diminutive reduplication copies H (gìlúlúmì) but inserts a default B where the base is B (gìmùmù:tù); a rising tone on a final vowel can arise from a structural tone plus an intonational tone (observed in Ndumu as in Teke, p. 172).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on nominal and verbal stems, cited in isolation and in presentative/aorist frames (Franceville Ndumu, informant from Epila; text from Albert Oyabi and clan elders). The statement establishes tonality only; the source is silent on stress, so the reading is 'tone language, no stress statement' rather than a stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Puech's data are Ndumu of the Franceville/Mpasa area (B63; informant born at Epila, kuya clan; text from Albert Oyabi and elders of the kaandjogo and kuya clans) = ndum1239. Mouele 1988 and Medjo Mvé 1989 describe the Lenyani (le-nyani) dialect of the same language; Pholia 1 lists 'epigi' as another Ndumu dialect. Puech 1987b labels the comparison language 'atege' (Teke of Djoko, B70), not Ndumu.

sources.note: Tone-marked oral text from Franceville Ndumu speakers; p. 143 + fn. 6 give the tonal notation (acute = H, grave = L, apostrophe = H with downstep, circumflex = falling, rising; unmarked final vowel not pronounced) and note that Adam's works never mark tones. Nothing said about stress/accent as prominence.

sources.citation: Mayer, Raymond & Hubert Binga. 1997. Trajets migratoires et parlers ndumu. Cahiers Gabonais d'Anthropologie 1: 61 ff. Libreville: Université Omar Bongo.
sources.note: Historical/oral-tradition reply to Puech 1987a (migration, dialect names, Ndumu texts collected in 1988); nothing on tone or stress.

Grepped for 'ndumu': only the Gabon language inventory and bibliography (Pholia 1: lists Biton 1903/1907/1923/1962, Adam 1950/1954/1969), Ndumu oral-tradition recordings (Pholia 4: 210-211), and Adam 1954/1969 cited for ideophones (Pholia 8). No Ndumu phonology and nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Puech, Gilbert. 1987b. Tons structurels et tons intonationnels en teke. Pholia 2: 163-173.
sources.note: Tonal comparison of Teke (atege, Djoko) with Ndumu (informant from Epila): both have H/B structural tones plus intonational tones; in Ndumu a floating H shifts right onto the radical vowel (bàlàgà -> bálàgà 'c'est un mâle', mù:tù -> mú:tù, pp. 165-166), downstep ('faille tonale') after H, verb stems split into B- and H-radical tone classes, diminutive reduplication copies H. No statement about word stress.
